document.title: Childhood trauma scores showed no meaningful link to amygdala-prefrontal coupling in 187 adults
document.standfirst: In a preregistered test on open brain-scan data, adults' childhood trauma questionnaire scores were unrelated to resting connectivity between the amygdala and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (partial r -0.006). The result rules out effects of 0.20 or larger and leaves smaller ones between 0.10 and 0.20 open.
document.tier_reason: A clean registered equivalence null on real CC0 data with a shuffled control. A larger null already exists, so it adds a replication and a specific equivalence bound. Power 0.77 at the bound, modest.
document.rung_reason: Prereg with fail-closed rules on file; no named rival beaten by a decisive observation.
document.bound: Correlations of 0.20 or larger in size are excluded at the preregistered bound (90 percent interval -0.129 to 0.117); true effects between 0.10 and 0.20 remain open.
document.objection: Anatomical mask, a low-pass FD rule outside its validated single-band data, retrospective self-report, and no positive control showing the pipeline finds a known effect.
document.would_change: Add a second open sample or functional vmPFC mask to shrink the 0.10 to 0.20 gap; add a positive control

sections.title: What this means for a reader
paragraphs: Small studies have reported that people who were maltreated as children show weaker resting coupling between the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex. In 187 adults, with the test fixed in advance, we found no association of a size that would matter, and a much larger study found the same in 1,325 adults. Treat a strong resting-state version of the claim with caution. A weak effect is still possible, two trauma subscales gave inconclusive results, and other kinds of brain measurement were not tested.

sections.title: Abstract
paragraphs: A widely discussed idea holds that childhood maltreatment weakens the coupling between the amygdala, which responds to threat, and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which helps regulate that response. We tested one resting-state form of the idea with the analysis fixed before any questionnaire value or image was seen. The data are the Transdiagnostic Connectome Project on OpenNeuro (CC0): 241 adults with and without psychiatric diagnoses, preprocessed in full, of whom 187 met the motion and questionnaire rules. {c1}Childhood trauma scores were unrelated to amygdala-vmPFC resting connectivity in 187 adults: partial r -0.006, 95% interval -0.152 to 0.140.{/c1} {c2}The 90% interval, -0.129 to 0.117, lies inside -0.20 to 0.20, so effects of 0.20 or larger in size are excluded at the preregistered bound.{/c2} A secondary region gave r -0.025. Shuffling the trauma scores 10,000 times placed the observed value at the 47th percentile. {c3}Fifteen exploratory sensitivity analyses moved the primary r between -0.081 and 0.081, and none reached an association.{/c3} {c4}The emotional-neglect and physical-abuse subscale analyses, r 0.081 and -0.081, are inconclusive because their 90% intervals touch 0.20.{/c4} {c5}Power to detect a correlation of 0.20 was 0.77, so true effects between 0.10 and 0.20 remain open.{/c5}

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: The {g:amygdala}amygdala{/g} and the {g:vmpfc}ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC){/g} form a circuit often linked to threat and its regulation. A common hypothesis is that maltreatment in childhood changes this circuit, and that the change shows up as weaker {g:rsfc}resting-state functional connectivity{/g} between the two.

Birn and colleagues {cite:r2} studied 27 male combat veterans, 17 of them with PTSD, and modelled amygdala and hippocampus connectivity from childhood maltreatment, combat exposure and PTSD symptoms together. Their abstract reports that scores on the {g:ctq}Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ){/g} predicted lower amygdala connectivity to the vmPFC.

Goltermann and colleagues {cite:r3} tested the same family of claims in 1,325 adults (624 with major depression, 701 healthy controls), with the CTQ and regions chosen from earlier reports, among them the amygdala. Maltreatment was not associated with the connectivity of any region of interest in the full sample. Within the depressed group, maltreatment went with greater, not weaker, connectivity between the amygdala and dorsolateral frontal areas. The authors conclude that most earlier connectivity correlates of maltreatment did not replicate.

Our study adds a smaller, independent test on open data with one feature the larger study did not state in its abstract: a preregistered {g:sesoi}smallest effect of interest{/g} and an {g:tost}equivalence test (two one-sided tests){/g} in the form Lakens {cite:r4} describes for correlations. An equivalence test can support "no effect of a size that matters", which a non-significant result alone cannot.

sections.title: Preregistration and design
paragraphs: The {g:preregistration}preregistration{/g} was frozen on 9 October 2026, before any phenotype value or image from the dataset was downloaded or viewed. Only file names, the dataset description and the CTQ definitions file had been read. Three choices were made at that point: an anatomical vmPFC, the full sample with no diagnostic filter, and a smallest effect of interest of 0.20 in size, about 4 percent shared variance.
The decision rule had three outcomes, fixed in advance:

- Association: the 95 percent interval excludes 0 and, by a {g:deviation}deviation{/g} logged before any data were processed, the {g:holm}Holm correction{/g}-adjusted p across the two registered tests is below 0.05.
- No meaningful association: the 90 percent interval lies wholly inside -0.20 to 0.20.
- Inconclusive: neither.
The preregistration also stated that effects between 0.10 and 0.20 could be missed at the expected sample size, and that any write-up must say so.
Six deviations are logged in the preregistration, each dated with the point at which it was decided:

- 1 to 3, on 9 October, before any participant was processed: keep aCompCor components up to five per mask when fewer are available; require the Holm-adjusted p for an association call; use each session's acquired field maps for distortion correction, with a field-map-free fallback where they do not match.
- 4, on 10 October: a fallback preprocessing path if a software licence was not in place. It was not used; every participant went through one pipeline.

- 5 and its correction 5a, on 10 October, after one participant's motion check and before any trauma or connectivity value was opened: the data are multiband with a 0.8 second repetition time, and breathing showed up as apparent motion. The motion rule became a 0.1 Hz low-pass filter on the motion parameters, with volumes censored above 0.1 mm, following Gratton and colleagues {cite:r5}. That rule was validated on single-band data, so here it runs outside its validated setting. Deviation 5 first specified a band-stop filter that did not remove the breathing signal; 5a replaced it.

- 6, on 29 October, after preprocessing and before any trauma-connectivity value was opened, decided from counts of the questionnaire coding only: the dataset codes missing CTQ answers as 88, which the registered code did not list, so 88 became a missing code.

sections.title: Data and provenance
paragraphs: The data are the Transdiagnostic Connectome Project, OpenNeuro dataset ds005237, snapshot 1.1.3 {cite:r1}, released under CC0, a public-domain dedication. It is a transdiagnostic adult sample with up to four resting-state runs per participant. This paper reports group statistics only; per-participant tables were not published and no individual record appears here.

All 241 participants were preprocessed with {g:fmriprep}fMRIPrep{/g} 25.2.6, with no processing errors. Of these, 230 had four runs, 6 had three and 5 had two. Distortion correction used acquired field maps for 198 participants and the field-map-free method for 43.

The analysed sample of 187 had a mean age of 33.4 years (SD 13.3). It included 112 women, 73 men and 2 people who reported another sex; 122 were scanned at one site and 65 at the other; 114 were in the patient group and 73 in the general-population group. The mean CTQ total was 43.0 (SD 17.3) on a scale of 25 to 125.

sections.title: Methods
paragraphs: ## Regions

Regions came from the {g:harvard-oxford}Harvard-Oxford atlas{/g} at the 50 percent threshold in standard space: left and right amygdala combined; "Frontal Medial Cortex" for the primary vmPFC target; and "Subcallosal Cortex", the label closest to Brodmann area 25, as the pre-declared secondary target.
## Denoising and motion

Each run was cleaned by regression of 24 motion parameters, {g:acompcor}aCompCor{/g} (up to five white-matter and five cerebrospinal-fluid components) and cosine drift terms, with no {g:gsr}global signal regression{/g} in the primary analysis. {g:fd}Framewise displacement{/g} was computed from low-pass filtered motion parameters, and {g:censoring}censoring{/g} removed volumes above 0.1 mm together with uncensored segments shorter than five volumes. A run was unusable with more than 20 percent of volumes censored, and a participant needed at least two usable runs.
## Connectivity
For each usable run {m:j}, {m:r_j} is the Pearson correlation of the mean denoised time series of the two regions. It is converted with the {g:fisher-z}Fisher z{/g} transform,
$$ z_j = \frac{1}{2} \ln \frac{1 + r_j}{1 - r_j} {eq:z}
and averaged over the participant's {m:R} usable runs:
$$ Z = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{j} z_j {eq:mean}
## The test

The exposure is the CTQ total, the sum of the five subscales. The statistic is the {g:partial-r}partial correlation{/g} {m:r_p} between CTQ total and {m:Z}, adjusting for age, sex, site, mean filtered framewise displacement and the number of retained volumes, which the result file records as {m:k = 6} model terms. Intervals use the Fisher transform of {m:r_p} with standard error
$$ SE = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n - 3 - k}} {eq:se}

and run from {m:z_p - c \cdot SE} to {m:z_p + c \cdot SE}, transformed back to the correlation scale, with {m:c} 1.96 for the 95 percent interval and 1.645 for the 90 percent interval. With {m:n = 187} this gives the intervals in Table {ref:tab:main}. {g:stat-power}Statistical power{/g} uses the same normal approximation.

sections.title: Controls and planted checks
paragraphs: The {g:control}control{/g} shuffled CTQ totals across participants 10,000 times (seed 20261029) and recomputed the partial correlation each time, giving a {g:null-distribution}null distribution{/g} for both the primary and the secondary test. It shows where the observed value sits among values that carry no link by construction.

There is no {g:positive-control}positive control{/g}. No known effect was planted in the data, and no {g:planted-check}planted check{/g} shows that this pipeline would find a connectivity effect of size 0.20 when one is present. The equivalence call rests on the interval width, which depends on the sample size and not on the pipeline's sensitivity. A pipeline that destroyed real signal would also produce a narrow interval around zero. This is the main weakness of the design.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: Of 241 participants, 17 were excluded for having fewer than two usable runs after motion censoring, 16 had no CTQ record and 21 were missing at least one subscale, leaving 187.

{c1}Childhood trauma scores were unrelated to amygdala-vmPFC resting connectivity in 187 adults: partial r -0.006, 95% interval -0.152 to 0.140.{/c1} {c2}The 90% interval, -0.129 to 0.117, lies inside -0.20 to 0.20, so effects of 0.20 or larger in size are excluded at the preregistered bound.{/c2} The decision is "no meaningful association". The secondary region gave the same decision (Table {ref:tab:main}).

::table tab:main cols=0.32,0.07,0.1,0.19,0.19,0.13 The two registered tests. Holm-adjusted p is across the two tests.
Test ¦ n ¦ Partial r ¦ 95% interval ¦ 90% interval ¦ Holm p
Primary, frontal medial cortex ¦ 187 ¦ -0.006 ¦ -0.152 to 0.140 ¦ -0.129 to 0.117 ¦ 1.0
Secondary, subcallosal cortex ¦ 187 ¦ -0.025 ¦ -0.171 to 0.121 ¦ -0.147 to 0.098 ¦ 1.0
::end

The unadjusted p values were 0.94 and 0.74. Under the shuffle control the primary value sat at the 47th percentile of 10,000 shuffles (two-sided permutation p 0.93) and the secondary at the 37th (p 0.73), as Figure {ref:fig:null} shows. The shuffled primary values ran from -0.119 to 0.124 between the 5th and 95th percentiles.

![fig:null width=0.98 alt=Two rows, each a diamond near zero inside a grey band of shuffled values](fig-null.png) Observed partial r (diamonds) against the 5th to 95th percentile (bar), 2.5th to 97.5th percentile (line) and median (tick) of 10,000 shuffles of CTQ scores across participants. Drawn from the study's group-level result file.

{c5}Power to detect a correlation of 0.20 was 0.77, so true effects between 0.10 and 0.20 remain open.{/c5} At the Holm-adjusted threshold the power was 0.68. The smallest correlation detectable with 80 percent power was 0.207. The chance that the equivalence test succeeds when the true correlation is zero was 0.71.

{c3}Fifteen exploratory sensitivity analyses moved the primary r between -0.081 and 0.081, and none reached an association.{/c3} Figure {ref:fig:forest} draws all of them with the two registered tests; Table {ref:tab:sens} in Appendix A lists them. Thirteen of the fifteen met the equivalence rule on the primary region. {c4}The emotional-neglect and physical-abuse subscale analyses, r 0.081 and -0.081, are inconclusive because their 90% intervals touch 0.20.{/c4} Their 90% intervals run from -0.041 to 0.201 and from -0.202 to 0.042. Each of these single subscales neither shows an association nor excludes one of 0.20.

The same sensitivity analyses were also run on the secondary region. Two of them were inconclusive there: the band-stop motion rule (n 131, r -0.110, 90% interval -0.253 to 0.039) and the sexual-abuse subscale (r -0.098, 90% interval -0.218 to 0.025). None reached an association.

![fig:forest width=0.92 alt=A forest plot of seventeen correlations near zero; two subscale rows in ochre reach the dashed 0.20 lines](fig-forest.png) Partial r with 90% intervals (thick) and 95% intervals (thin) for the two registered tests (top) and the fifteen exploratory sensitivity analyses on the primary region. The shaded band is the preregistered equivalence region, -0.20 to 0.20. Ochre marks an inconclusive result. Drawn from the study's group-level result files.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: The registered result is an {g:honest-null}honest null{/g} with a stated bound. Within this sample and this measure, the correlation between CTQ total and amygdala-vmPFC resting connectivity is smaller than 0.20 in size. That is consistent with Goltermann and colleagues {cite:r3}, whose abstract reports no maltreatment association with the connectivity of its regions of interest in 1,325 adults.

It does not contradict Birn and colleagues {cite:r2} directly. Their sample was 27 male veterans, most with PTSD, and their model held combat exposure and PTSD symptoms fixed alongside maltreatment; ours is a mixed transdiagnostic sample, mostly women and men, with demographic and motion covariates. An effect confined to a population like theirs could exist and be diluted here. The difference in design is the main reason the two results can both stand.

The inconclusive subscale results deserve plain reporting. Emotional neglect and physical abuse gave correlations of opposite sign, each with a 90 percent interval that crosses 0.20 by a small margin. They come from fifteen exploratory analyses with no correction, so one or two such edges are expected by chance. They do not support an association, and they also do not let us extend the equivalence claim to each subscale.

The deeper limit is the missing positive control. A null from a pipeline never shown to detect a known effect is weaker than a null from one that has. Adding one, for example a well-replicated connectivity difference with age or between homologous regions, is the next step before this pipeline is used for further trauma questions.

sections.title: Limitations
paragraphs: - One resting-state measure, with anatomical masks, in one transdiagnostic adult sample. Task-evoked regulation and other connectivity methods were not tested.
- The CTQ is retrospective self-report.
- The primary motion rule uses a low-pass filter on framewise displacement outside the single-band data it was validated on.
- There is no positive control, so the pipeline's ability to find a known effect is not shown.
- A true correlation between 0.10 and 0.20 in size could give this result; power at 0.20 was 0.77.
- Two subscale analyses on the primary region and two analyses on the secondary region were inconclusive.
- The analysis was run by our own code and was not blind.

steps: Preprocess with fMRIPrep 25.2.6 into standard space. Denoise with 24 motion parameters, aCompCor and cosine terms. Censor volumes with low-pass filtered framewise displacement above 0.1 mm and segments shorter than five volumes; drop runs with more than 20 percent censored; keep participants with at least two usable runs.
Extract mean time series from the Harvard-Oxford amygdala and Frontal Medial Cortex masks at the 50 percent threshold, correlate, apply eq. {ref:eq:z} and average with eq. {ref:eq:mean}.
Sum the five CTQ subscales, treating 88 as missing. Compute the partial correlation with the six covariate terms and its intervals with eq. {ref:eq:se}, then apply the decision rule at 0.20.
Shuffle CTQ totals 10,000 times with seed 20261029 for the null.
